https://www.dw.com/en/jason-arday-ex-cam.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IrbN Arday, was a professor of sociology of education [FILE: July 23, 2012] Image: Joe Giddens/LOCOG/PA/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Jason Arday, the former University of Cambridge professor who resigned amid allegations of plagiarism, was found dead on Friday. Without naming him directly, the Metropolitan Police said he was found "unresponsive" in Battersea, south London , and pronounced dead at the scene. "At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," a spokesperson said. "His next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by officers." Arday, a professor of sociology of education at Cambridge, one of the world's top universities, resigned just over a week ago amid mounting allegations that he plagiarized parts of his PhD thesis and overstated his personal achievements. He had denied wrongdoing, saying in a resignation letter last week that he did not accept "the narratives that have surrounded me." Questions mounted over thesis and fundraising claims British newspapers and commentators have seized on the allegations, arguing that he gained an unfair advantage through diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies. Scrutiny of Arday's credentials intensified last month after criticism from former Cambridge researcher Nathan Cofnas. The Times of London later reported similarities between passages in Arday's 2015 PhD thesis and an earlier paper by another researcher. Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated and cleared by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate. But last week, Cambridge launched an investigation following "new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments." British media also questioned Arday's claims of having raised £5.5 million (€6.4 million, $7.4 million) for charity through endurance challenges. Arday told The Guardian the funds were raised collectively over two decades. Supporters reject claims, cite racial bias Supporters, including over two dozen academics and politicians, characterized the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to discredit Arday and other Black people in influential positions. In his resignation letter, Arday said that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love." His family issued a statement denouncing the "campaign of sustained abuse" Arday had faced since he took the role at Cambridge University more than three years ago. "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," Arday's family said. "We won't comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long," the statement added. Cambridge's Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice said, "We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time." Edited by: Rob Turner and Karl Sexton Don't let the algorithm hide the news. Photograph: Brigida Sanchez/U.S. Army Corps of Engineers/AP Trump administration Trump names Adam Telle as acting army secretary following departure of Dan Driscoll Telle has previously worked for Trump during his first term as a special assistant to the president for legislative affairs Associated Press Thu 3 Sep 2026 20.18 EDT Last modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 20.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump on Thursday named Adam Telle as the acting army secretary after the departure of Daniel Driscoll amid widespread reports of tensions with defense secretary Pete Hegseth . Telle is currently the assistant secretary of the army for civil works. “He is a Great Patriot, who is respected by all,” the US president wrote in a Truth Social post. Driscoll gave no explanation for his decision to quit this week as the army’s top civilian official. His clashes with Hegseth have been widely reported, and some of Driscoll’s allies in the army were ousted this year by Trump’s Pentagon chief. Democrats warn of ‘hollowed out’ leadership after army chief resigns amid clashes with Hegseth Read more Telle has been at the Army Office of Civil Works since August 2025, according to Legistorm, a website that tracks lawmakers and Capitol Hill staffers. Before that, Telle spent 20 years mostly working in Congress for lawmakers, including as chief of staff for Republican Senator Bill Hagerty of Tennessee from 2021 to 2025. Telle had a job for 18 months working in the White House during Trump’s first term as a special assistant to the president for legislative affairs, Legistorm said. He also spent more than 10 years working for the late Republican Senator Thad Cochran of Mississippi. Telle will be overseeing the country’s largest fighting force at a time when the US is still engaged in conflict with Iran and significant army forces are stationed in the Middle East. The war has significantly contributed to the US military’s shortfall in critical weapons like the Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (Thaad) missile interceptor systems, which are operated by the army. Driscoll, an army veteran who served in Iraq, did not offer an explanation for why he stepped down after 18 months as the service’s civilian leader. He is a friend of vice-president JD Vance and had good relationships with both Republicans and Democrats in Congress. His allies in the army who were ousted by Hegseth included its top uniformed leader, Gen Randy George. Gen Christopher LaNeve took over as the army’s acting chief of staff and recently pulled the plug on a drone modernization program that Driscoll had championed. Driscoll spoke with Trump on the current state of the army before he submitted his resignation, the Associated Press has reported. Driscoll did not allude to any problems in the only public statement on his departure, saying Tuesday that it has been “the honor of a lifetime” to serve as army secretary under Trump and Hegseth. “We could not have made the progress we did without the support of secretary Hegseth,” he added. Democrats and Republicans lamented Driscoll’s departure, with some blaming Hegseth directly. Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who is retiring and sometimes has clashed with Trump, said on social media that Hegseth “is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks”.
